2. ABSTRACT
Standard Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) paradigms face an acute operational trade-off between
localized retrieval efficiency and high-level, holistic synthesis. Conventional Dense Vector RAG operates over
discrete text passages indexed via semantic embeddings, providing millisecond-scale latency and minimal
compute overhead for factual queries; however, it suffers from severe semantic myopia, rendering it incapable of
synthesizing cross-document themes, global trends, or holistic summaries. In contrast, graph-based RAG
architectures (GraphRAG) extract entity-relation knowledge graphs and compute hierarchical community
summaries via modularity clustering, unlocking broad corpus-wide thematic summarization. Yet, deploying
GraphRAG across enterprise workloads induces an unsustainable 10× to 20× inflation in LLM token expenditures
and orders of magnitude higher latency, even for elementary pinpoint lookups. To resolve this fundamental dichotomy, AdaptiRAG v1.0 introduces an adaptive hybrid architecture
governed by an intelligent, pre-retrieval Query Classifier (Router Agent). The router dynamically intercepts
incoming natural language queries and directs them to the optimal engine: specific factual and pinpoint inquiries
are serviced via a high-performance FAISS FlatIP dense vector index, whereas broad thematic queries invoke a
multi-tiered Neo4j knowledge graph traversed through Leiden-based community hierarchical map-reduce
synthesis. 10/17/26, 6:17 PM AdaptiRAG v1.0 - Comprehensive Academic Project Synopsis 2
Furthermore, AdaptiRAG addresses critical shortcomings in existing knowledge graph architectures by
engineering a temporal grounding engine enforcing closed validity intervals [τstart, τend] on graph edges,

symmetric order-swapped and length-normalized LLM-as-a-Judge benchmarking framework to ensure unbiased
empirical evaluation. The target outcome is a 68.4% reduction in query token expenditures and a drop in local

3. INTRODUCTION AND BACKGROUND
Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated extraordinary generative and contextual reasoning
capabilities across technical domains. However, when deployed in mission-critical environments, foundational
LLMs remain susceptible to hallucinations, factual inaccuracies, and severe knowledge cutoff boundaries. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) emerged as the dominant architecture to mitigate these failure modes by
dynamically grounding generation in external, domain-specific corpora. The traditional baseline, Vector RAG, decomposes documents into contiguous token chunks (e.g., 512
tokens), embeds them into dense vector spaces via models like text-embedding-ada-002 or open-source
equivalents, and queries an approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) index using cosine similarity. While exceptional
at locating exact keyword matches and local semantic clusters, this paradigm exhibits fundamental structural
blindness. Queries requiring holistic aggregation—such as "What are the central themes and evolving strategic
risks across the entire corpus?"—fail completely under dense retrieval because the constituent evidence is
dispersed across hundreds of non-contiguous passages that cannot be captured within standard top-k similarity
bounds. To address this limitation, GraphRAG constructs an intermediate structured representation: an LLM extracts
entity-relationship-claim triples, builds a knowledge graph, executes community detection algorithms (such as the
Leiden or Louvain algorithms) to form hierarchical topic clusters, and pre-generates hierarchical community
reports. While GraphRAG successfully achieves high-level thematic synthesis, forcing every incoming user query
through heavy graph traversals and map-reduce LLM cascades is computationally profligate and economically
unviable for practical deployment. Empirical workload distributions in enterprise environments demonstrate that real-world queries are
heterogeneous: approximately 60–75% of queries are localized factual questions, while 25–40% represent broad
comparative or thematic inquiries. AdaptiRAG models retrieval as a dynamic routing and constraint-satisfaction
problem, routing queries down the lowest-cost path capable of satisfying information requirements while
maintaining strict temporal validity and verifiable attribution. 10/17/26, 6:17 PM AdaptiRAG v1.0 - Comprehensive Academic Project Synopsis 3
4. PROBLEM STATEMENT AND RESEARCH GAPS
Existing RAG architectures force system designers into an uncompromising trade-off between shallow, low-cost
retrieval and deep, prohibitively expensive synthesis. AdaptiRAG isolates and targets four foundational research
gaps:
1. Semantic Myopia in Vector RAG: Dense vector retrieval relies strictly on pointwise proximity in
embedding space. Because embeddings are generated on localized chunks, they lack global structural
topology. Consequently, Vector RAG cannot perform multi-hop deductive reasoning or corpus-wide
synthesis, frequently omitting cross-document context. 2. Prohibitive Latency and Inference Costs in GraphRAG: Static GraphRAG pipelines subject all queries—
regardless of complexity—to community map-reduce passes. This introduces excessive query latency (p95 of
~1,840 ms compared to 118 ms for vector lookup) and escalates LLM token consumption by 10×–20×,
causing unsustainable financial and computational overhead on simple factual questions. 3. Temporal Inconsistency and Hallucination in Static Knowledge Graphs: Real-world corpora (such as
financial quarterly disclosures, regulatory statutes, and engineering specifications) are inherently time-
variant. Conventional knowledge graphs flatten historical facts into static edges without temporal qualifiers.

parses documents into 512-token chunks (with 64-token overlap) indexed via a FAISS FlatIP vector database,

Introduction and Company Profile 1.1 Purpose of the Study Product and brand management connects what a firm makes with what customers believe about it. This mini project applies that idea to a real organisation. It begins with the full product mix of a company, narrows down to one flagship product, and then examines that product through the lenses of the product life cycle (PLC), brand equity, market segmentation and brand positioning. The report ends with practical recommendations for managing the brand’s associations, loyalty and positioning. 1.2 Why Amul? Amul, marketed by the Gujarat Co-operative Milk Marketing Federation Ltd. (GCMMF), was selected because it satisfies every selection condition in the course guidelines. It has a wide and visible product portfolio spanning milk, butter, cheese, ghee, ice cream, chocolates and more. It has strong, easily observable brand communication, including the long-running Amul Girl advertising. It is also available on every channel a student can observe: neighbourhood shops, supermarkets, e-commerce and quick-commerce apps. From the portfolio, Amul Butter is chosen as the flagship product for deeper analysis because it is the brand’s most iconic product, it has a long history, and it faces visible competition. 1.3 Company Profile Amul began in 1946 as a farmers’ cooperative in Anand, Gujarat, formed so that small dairy farmers could sell milk directly and fairly instead of depending on private traders. Under the leadership of Dr. Verghese Kurien, it grew into the model behind India’s “White Revolution”. Today GCMMF is described as the world’s largest farmer-owned dairy cooperative and markets its products under the Amul brand. District milk unions process the milk and manufacture dairy products. GCMMF, at the state level, markets all products under one brand through a common distribution network. Farmers receive a large share of what the consumer pays, which keeps the supply base motivated and gives the brand a strong “farmer-owned” story. Because the cooperative returns surplus to farmers instead of maximising shareholder profit, it can price products competitively and still invest in processing, cold-chain and advertising. 1.5 Target Markets Mass consumers: households across urban and rural India who buy milk, butter, ghee, curd and cheese as daily staples. Introduction and Company Profile 1.1 Purpose of the Study Product and brand management connects what a firm makes with what customers believe about it. This mini project applies that idea to a real organisation. It begins with the full product mix of a company, narrows down to one flagship product, and then examines that product through the lenses of the product life cycle (PLC), brand equity, market segmentation and brand positioning. The report ends with practical recommendations for managing the brand’s associations, loyalty and positioning. 1.2 Why Amul? Amul, marketed by the Gujarat Co-operative Milk Marketing Federation Ltd. (GCMMF), was selected because it satisfies every selection condition in the course guidelines. It has a wide and visible product portfolio spanning milk, butter, cheese, ghee, ice cream, chocolates and more. It has strong, easily observable brand communication, including the long-running Amul Girl advertising. It is also available on every channel a student can observe: neighbourhood shops, supermarkets, e-commerce and quick-commerce apps. From the portfolio, Amul Butter is chosen as the flagship product for deeper analysis because it is the brand’s most iconic product, it has a long history, and it faces visible competition. 1.3 Company Profile Amul began in 1946 as a farmers’ cooperative in Anand, Gujarat, formed so that small dairy farmers could sell milk directly and fairly instead of depending on private traders. Under the leadership of Dr. Verghese Kurien, it grew into the model behind India’s “White Revolution”. Today GCMMF is described as the world’s largest farmer-owned dairy cooperative and markets its products under the Amul brand. District milk unions process the milk and manufacture dairy products. GCMMF, at the state level, markets all products under one brand through a common distribution network. Farmers receive a large share of what the consumer pays, which keeps the supply base motivated and gives the brand a strong “farmer-owned” story. Because the cooperative returns surplus to farmers instead of maximising shareholder profit, it can price products competitively and still invest in processing, cold-chain and advertising. 1.5 Target Markets Mass consumers: households across urban and rural India who buy milk, butter, ghee, curd and cheese as daily staples. Young and urban consumers: buyers of ice cream, flavoured milk, cheese, protein products and ready-to-eat items, increasingly through quick-commerce and e-commerce. Institutional buyers: restaurants, bakeries, caterers and pizza chains that use butter, cheese and cream in bulk. International consumers: the Indian diaspora and other buyers abroad, where Amul has begun selling fresh milk and other products. 1.6 Scope, Method and Assumptions The study uses secondary data: company announcements, news reports, industry and brand-valuation reports, and observation of product listings and packaging. Busy working professionals, students and parents preparing tiffins often leave it out to soften, which is inconvenient and can affect freshness and hygiene. Many also want smaller, controlled portions. Proposed product: Amul Soft Butter Spread (concept) A dairy spread that stays soft and spreadable straight from the refrigerator, offered in a tub and a squeezable resealable pack. Proposed variants are Salted, Garlic-Herb, Chilli-Garlic and Lite. It keeps the Amul taste and the “pure dairy” promise, but removes the main usage frustration. Similar spreadable butters already exist in international markets, which shows the need is real. How it can be developed The softness can be achieved through dairy-based techniques such as controlling the fat composition of the cream or butter, which Amul’s dairy technology teams are well placed to do. Pack design must protect freshness and allow clean dispensing. The product must also comply with food-labelling and standards rules set by the food regulator (FSSAI). This is the closest published relative of AdaptiRAG's learned router. Problem
Vanilla RAG handles single-hop queries well but struggles with multi-hop reasoning. Graph RAG handles
multi-hop but adds construction and retrieval cost. Existing hybrids either always call graph retrieval, or route
with heuristics (such as entity counts) that generalize poorly, or with an LLM classifier whose cost can approach
the pipeline it is meant to save. Method  Router: DeBERTa-v3-base with a linear layer and sigmoid giving two scores, vanilla-suitability and
graph-suitability. Trained with focal binary cross-entropy (alpha 0.25, gamma 2.0). Routes to graph RAG if
graph score minus vanilla score exceeds a threshold tau, tuned on validation over [0.0, 0.5] to maximize (F1
+ Recall)/2 for the graph class, weighting recall because sending a graph-needing query to vanilla is the
costlier error.  Rewriter (LLM, only when needed): if a query goes to graph RAG with graph confidence below 0.6, it is
decomposed into [head, relation, tail] triplets with unknown intermediate entities as placeholders. The query
becomes the original plus the triplet chain.  Control flow: route; if vanilla, answer; if graph, rewrite only when uncertain, then run graph RAG. Tech stack used

2. Abstract
AdaptiRAG v1.0 is a hybrid retrieval-augmented generation system that routes each query to the cheapest retrieval method able to answer it well. Vector RAG is fast but retrieves only local chunks, so it fails on corpus-wide summarization. GraphRAG handles global themes through hierarchical
community summaries, but costs 10×–20× more LLM tokens, even on simple factual questions. The project adds a pre-retrieval Query Classifier that sends factual queries to a FAISS vector index and thematic queries to a Neo4j graph with Leiden
community map-reduce. The graph stores closed validity intervals [τstart, τend] on facts, so time-bound questions do not mix old and current
information. A position-swapped, length-normalized LLM-as-a-Judge framework evaluates all systems fairly. The targeted outcome is a large cut in query token cost and latency versus pure GraphRAG, while keeping its comprehensiveness and diversity on
global queries. 3. Introduction and Background
Retrieval-Augmented Generation grounds a Large Language Model (LLM) in external documents. The standard approach, Vector RAG, embeds
document chunks and retrieves the nearest ones by cosine similarity. This works well for specific lookups but struggles with questions such as "What
are the main themes across this corpus?", because the answer is spread over many passages that no single similarity search will return together. GraphRAG addresses this by extracting entities and relationships into a knowledge graph, clustering it into communities with the Leiden algorithm,
and summarizing each community. Global questions are then answered by a map-reduce over these summaries. The trade-off is heavy indexing and
inference cost. Most real workloads mix both query types. A system that always uses GraphRAG overpays on simple questions, and one that always uses Vector RAG
fails on broad ones. AdaptiRAG treats this as a routing problem and also addresses two further weaknesses of current systems: temporal
inconsistency in the graph and biased LLM-based evaluation. 4. Problem Statement and Research Gaps
Existing RAG systems force a choice between cheap-but-shallow and deep-but-expensive retrieval, and the way they are compared is itself unreliable. The project targets four gaps:

The first responsibility is operational excellence: dependable mail processing, equipment servicing, customer support, financial controls and safe facilities. The second is renewal: modern SaaS products, API-based integrations, analytics, automation and better digital experiences. These two responsibilities should not compete for attention. A stable core creates trust and funds innovation; innovation can in turn simplify the core. For example, a better customer portal can reduce avoidable calls, while cleaner service data can improve both customer communication and internal planning. 4.3 Key enablers and success factors Leadership alignment: executives should agree on a small number of measurable outcomes, such as customer effort, on-time processing, cost per item and service reliability. Digital talent: teams need cloud engineering, cybersecurity, data analytics, automation, product management and frontline process knowledge. Technology architecture: systems should use secure APIs, common data standards and modular integration so that legacy systems can be modernised in manageable stages. Culture and adoption: frontline employees should be involved in design and testing; training should explain how new tools change daily work. Governance: assign owners for data quality, AI model monitoring, cyber risk, vendor performance and benefits realisation. Customer feedback: use customer interviews, service cases and product usage data to decide which improvements matter most. 4.4 Legacy modernisation needs The SAP customer case describes Pitney Bowes’ effort to replace an ageing on-premise ERP solution and consolidate parts of its IT landscape in selected countries. First map critical processes and dependencies; then clean master data; standardise workflows; expose stable services through APIs; migrate suitable workloads; and retire redundant applications only after users and controls are ready. 4.5 Major barriers and responses 4.6 Strategic interpretation The company’s transformation should be treated as a portfolio of connected improvements rather than one large technology project.
